From a saved flow to the verbs Jambonz plays: the compiler, the webhook exchange, and the
limits on each hook. The internals behind each step are in
docs/internals/runtime.md and
docs/internals/compiler.md (indexed from AGENTS.md).

## Compiler pipeline

```
raw JSON / dict
     │
     ▼
[1] Normalizer:   Apply each component type's defaults across the tree
     │
     ▼
[2] Validator:    Per-component checks, branch-outlet legality, goto targets
     │
     ▼
[3] CodeGen:      Flatten the component tree → flat node_map of Jambonz verb dicts
     │            keyed by dotted-path ids (main.menu.tsales), with routing metadata
     ▼
[4] Graph:        Synchronous cycle detection over the flattened map
     │
     ▼
[5] Pipeline:     Assemble CompiledFlow (4 handler entry ids) → CompilerResult
```

## The webhook exchange

Jambonz is **stateless**; each call leg is a series of HTTP webhook exchanges:

```
Inbound call
    │
    ▼ POST /webhooks/{flow_name}
Execute from the main entry node
    → Accumulate Jambonz verbs
    → Stop at a blocking component (menu/collect_input/voice_input/transfer/sip_refer/
      enqueue/dequeue/conference/ai_agent)
    → Return verb array (with an actionHook URL carrying the node's dotted id)
    │
    ▼ POST /webhooks/{flow_name}/continue/{node_id}
    (Jambonz sends gathered digits/speech, dial_call_status, queue_result /
     dequeue_result, refer_status)
Resolve the branch (digit → invalid → default; dial status → success/failure/timeout;
queue outcome → the outlet of that name; no input → timeout), resume execution
    → Return next verb array
```

**A Jambonz application has two webhooks, and both point here**: the *calling webhook*
(`/webhooks/{flow_name}`) and the *call status webhook* (`/webhooks/{flow_name}/callstatus`).
There is no error or disconnect hook in Jambonz, so:

- the **Error** handler runs when a component fails (on whichever hook that happens);
- the **Call Status** handler runs on every status event of the call (`{{call_status}}`
  says which: `trying`, `ringing`, `early-media`, `in-progress`, then `completed` /
  `failed` / `busy` / `no-answer`), but only for **the leg the flow drives**: the status
  hook also hears every leg a Transfer dials, and those (the ones carrying a
  `parent_call_sid`) are ignored;
- the **Disconnect** handler runs once, from the call status webhook, on the call's final
  status. Without the call status webhook configured, neither of the last two runs.

`/error` and `/disconnect` still answer, for deployments that point something at them,
but nothing in Jambonz calls them. A named subflow runs at `/subflows/{subflow_name}`.
Jambonz also fetches the flow's **application environment variables** with an `OPTIONS`
request to `/webhooks/{flow_name}`. The full route list is in [API.md](/reference/api/).

**Hooks are not idempotent, and Jambonz's retry option stays on the call webhook.**
Jambonz waits about 10 s for a hook and does not retry unless the URL carries a `#rc=`
fragment (`#rc=2&rp=ct`). Such a fragment on the calling webhook applies to that request
only: the continuation URLs this app hands back (`/continue/…`) carry none. That is on
purpose: a resumed hook re-run would capture the input and run the flow's side effects
(HTTP requests, SMS, logs) a second time.

## Subflows call and return

A `subflow` component runs the named subflow and, when the subflow reaches its end
(right away or after any number of menus and transfers), the call continues with the
component after it. The return address rides on the call with the other variables, and
one subflow can be used from as many places as you like. Calls nest; a subflow that calls
itself (directly or through others) is refused at save. Inside a subflow, **Exit Call
Flow** and **Disconnect** end the whole call, and a **Connector** to a component outside
the subflow leaves it for good (nothing returns afterwards).

## Call state

Call context (variables, digits, from/to) **rides on the call, not in the manager**:
before each suspension a `tag` verb persists the working variables under
`customerData.internal`, which Jambonz echoes back on the next webhook. The driver holds
no local call state, so a restarted instance picks up calls already in progress. That is
not a licence to run several: the file store is single-writer, every instance takes an
exclusive lock on its store directory, and an instance on a *copy* of the store has its
own writable editor that diverges from the first save; so run exactly one instance per
store. See [OPERATIONS.md](/reference/operations/#one-instance-per-store).

## Limits on one hook

**Three guards bound one hook.** `_MAX_ITERATIONS` caps how many nodes may run (a
runaway run is discarded and the flow's Error handler runs instead); `MAX_HOOK_SECONDS`
caps how long they may take; and `WEBHOOK_MAX_CONCURRENCY` caps how many hooks execute at
once, shedding rather than queueing beyond it.

**Jambonz waits about 10 seconds for a hook's answer** (the feature server's
`JAMBONES_HTTP_TIMEOUT`) and does not retry: an answer after that reaches nobody, and the
caller hears the line drop. So `MAX_HOOK_SECONDS` defaults to **8**: every `http_request`
ends by the end of that budget (or its own `HTTP_REQUEST_TIMEOUT`, whichever is sooner,
failing into `{{http_error}}` like any timeout); past it the hook routes to the flow's Error
handler, which runs on what is *left* of the same budget rather than a fresh one, as does
the Disconnect handler the call-status hook runs after its Call Status handler. A hook
as a whole therefore answers within about 8 s. Raising the budget above ~9 s buys nothing,
because Jambonz has stopped waiting. A shed hook that a caller is listening to answers
with a short apology and a hangup; the disconnect/call-status notifications answer `503`.
Every shed answer carries the header `X-Jamhooks-Shed: 1`, which is how the load test
([OPERATIONS.md](/reference/operations/#capacity-and-sizing)) counts them.

## Logging

**Every log line names its call.** Each hook opens a call scope, so `flow`, `call_sid`,
`hook` and the current `node_id` are stamped onto every record written beneath it,
including from a flow's own Log nodes and from third-party libraries. With
`LOG_FORMAT=json` they are top-level fields, so `call_sid:"..."` is the query that
answers "what happened on this call?". Every hook also ends with one completion line,
the deployment's metrics source ([OPERATIONS.md](/reference/operations/#health-and-logs)).

**Every routing decision is a line too** (logger `app.routing`): `waiting` when a hook
leaves the call waiting at a component (a Menu, User Input, Transfer, queue, …), and
`routed` when that answer comes back, or when a Conditional or Date & Time picks its
branch on the way. Each carries the component (`node_id`, `node_type`, its `label`) and,
when routed, a `result` (what happened, in the component's outlet names: `2`,
`timeout`, `invalid`, `failure`, `hangup`, a rule's key with its name in
`result_label`) and an `outlet`, the branch the call took (the result's own when it is
wired; else the fallback, or `next`, `end`, `error_handler`). Never the digits or speech
themselves. Only a real call writes them: Simulate runs the same steps and writes none.
The dashboard's Routing panels read them
([OPERATIONS.md](/reference/operations/#reading-the-routing-panels)).

## Live debugging

The editor's **Debug** tab (in the right-hand sidebar, node-red style, beside Simulate)
streams what real calls are doing to this flow, as they do it: per node, the outcome, the
verbs emitted and any unresolved `{{vars}}`, then a closing line per webhook with what
went back to Jambonz. Rows are grouped by call, and a filter narrows them to a call sid,
a node or a hook. It is the deployed counterpart to **Simulate** (the same per-node
record, from a real call) and usually the fastest way to answer "why did this caller
end up in the wrong branch?".

**Nothing is stored, anywhere.** Events are pushed over a websocket
(`/ws/trace/{flow_id}`) to whoever is watching and then forgotten: no buffer, no history,
no catch-up. A call that happens while nobody is watching leaves no trace, and the rows
you can see live only in your browser tab, capped at the most recent 300.

**The pane's Start button is what switches tracing on**, not opening the tab. The pane
starts detached; **Start** attaches it, and tracing runs for a flow exactly while at least
one pane is attached to it, held in memory. Once attached it stays attached while you
switch sidebar tabs or select components (which brings up Properties), and reconnects if
the connection drops. **Stop** detaches it, and so does leaving or closing the page, or
the sign-in ending. There is no setting to enable and forget about: with nobody
watching, the runtime builds no trace at all, so an untraced call costs a dictionary
lookup. `CALL_TRACE_ENABLED=false` is the deployment's veto: the socket then refuses
every connection, for a deployment that will not have live call data on a screen at all.

The socket authenticates itself (session login, or the trusted header when auth is
delegated), and read-only accounts may watch. It has to: **neither the auth beforeware nor
any middleware in this app runs for a websocket scope.**
